To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
English- and Mandarin-speaking infants differ in their abilities to learn new words for actions and for objects at 14 and 16 months of age.

1) English learners at 18 months of but not 14 months are able to map novel nouns and verbs to objects and actions, respectively; 2) Mandarin learners at both ages are able to map verbs to actions but not nouns to objects, and 3) the differences between English and Mandarin learners are consistent with those obtained in naturalistic and checklist studies.

English and Mandarin learning infants differ in their ability to learn novel labels for actions versus objects, and that these differences are consistent with the findings of previous naturalistic studies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of language-specific constraints in the early mapping of words to referents.
the development of word learning and the role of culture in shaping the course of development.
the development of the ability to learn words in a novel context, which is the focus of the current research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
English-learning infants learn words for actions earlier than for objects, and Mandarin-learning infants learn words only for actions, not objects.

the mapping of novel words to actions and objects varies as a function of language and developmental age, with a more rapid mapping of actions than objects in English learners and a more rapid mapping to actions than objects in Mandarin learners.

there is evidence for cross-linguistics differences between English and Mandarin learners in the mapping of novel words to objects, and that the difference is more robust in the mapping of nouns than verbs, but that the difference is not as clear cut as in previous research based on naturalistic or checklist methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
English learners are more likely to map words to both actions and nouns, whereas Mandarin learners are more likely map words to actions but not nouns.
English learners may be better equipped to learn object names, whereas Mandarin learners may have a better ability to learn action names.
the learning mechanisms are the same, but the weighting and recruitment of those mechanisms are influenced by language and culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mapping of words onto actions versus objects is a dynamic process that unfolds over development.
the mechanisms of word learning are not universal across cultures, but are shaped by the linguistic and cultural contexts in which they develop.
